title: Anurag Kashyap Is Finally Ready to Make Films Outside India — And Cannes 2026 Is Where It Starts
excerpt: After 20 years of saying no to international projects, the Gangs of Wasseypur director is taking meetings, writing the Sourav Ganguly biopic, and calling out India's Cannes red carpet obsession
body:
## The Enfant Terrible Goes Global

Anurag Kashyap has spent two decades being Indian cinema's most reliably provocative voice — the guy who made *Gangs of Wasseypur* feel like a religious experience and turned *Sacred Games* into India's first genuine prestige TV export. Now, walking the corridors of the Palais des Festivals at Cannes 2026, he's doing something he's never done before: saying yes.

"I am meeting filmmakers who have forever been chasing me from outside India to make a film, and I've been saying no because I am such a Banarasi boy," Kashyap told reporters at Cannes this week. "I had learnt how to speak English after so long, so how will I speak French or any other language and make a film! But today I am meeting people, and discussing if my ideas can translate."

For anyone who has followed Kashyap's career — from the banned *Paanch* to the underground cult of *Black Friday* to the global phenomenon of *Wasseypur* — this is a seismic shift. The man who once defined himself through his refusal to leave the gullies of Banaras and Dhanbad is now actively exploring international co-productions.

## "I Realised I Live in a Cave Too"

Kashyap, never one to spare himself from his own sharp tongue, offered a characteristically self-aware reflection on his evolution. "A few years ago I said Aditya Chopra lives in a cave, but I realised so do I!" he said, acknowledging that his insularity, once a creative strength, had become a limitation.

The catalyst? Watching Iranian master **Asghar Farhadi** — whose *A Separation* and *The Salesman* redefined what non-English cinema could achieve at the Oscars — premiere "Parallel Tales," a film made entirely in French. If Farhadi could cross linguistic borders without losing his artistic DNA, Kashyap reasoned, why couldn't he?

It's the kind of creative restlessness that has always defined Kashyap at his best. This isn't a filmmaker chasing Hollywood dollars. This is an artist recognising that stories about power, corruption, love, and survival don't need subtitles to be universal — they just need a storyteller brave enough to trust that.

## Back in the Groove — and Writing Everything

While the international pivot grabs headlines, Kashyap's current workload tells an equally compelling story. He's currently writing dialogues for **Vikramaditya Motwane's** upcoming *Dada*, the Sourav Ganguly biopic — a project that has cricket-loving desis worldwide already debating casting choices. He's also writing projects for **Luv Ranjan**, **Akiv Ali**, and **Nikhil Mahajan**, a workload that has him feeling like it's 2002 all over again.

"I am back in the groove, just like I was in 2001-2003 when I was writing for Mani Ratnam, Shankar, Vidhu Vinod Chopra, or Ram Gopal Verma," he said. For context, that early-2000s writing binge eventually produced *Black Friday*, *Dev.D*, and the screenplay for *Yuva*. When Kashyap says he's in the groove, history suggests you should pay attention.

## The Cannes Red Carpet Problem

True to form, Kashyap also took a swipe at India's increasingly performative relationship with the Cannes Film Festival. While Indian media breathlessly covers which actress wore what lehenga on the red carpet, Kashyap pointed out that the festival is supposed to be about cinema.

It's a critique that resonates particularly with the diaspora. NRIs who grew up on *Dev.D* and binge-watched *Sacred Games* in their college dorms want to see India represented at Cannes through filmmaking, not fashion spreads. Kashyap's presence at the festival as a working filmmaker — taking meetings, developing international projects, writing furiously — is the kind of representation that actually matters.

## What This Means for Desi Storytelling Abroad

For the global Indian diaspora, Kashyap going international isn't just one director's career move — it's a signal. If the filmmaker behind *Gangs of Wasseypur* believes desi stories can work on a global canvas without being diluted, it opens a door that filmmakers like **Neeraj Ghaywan**, **Zoya Akhtar**, and **Shoojit Sircar** might walk through next.

And then there's the Ganguly biopic. For cricket-obsessed NRIs — which is to say, most NRIs — a Kashyap-written Sourav Ganguly film directed by Motwane is the kind of project that sells itself. The shirt-waving at Lord's. The captaincy battles with Greg Chappell. The comeback. If Kashyap brings even half the raw energy of *Wasseypur* to Dada's dialogue, it could be special.

## What's Next

Kashyap remains at Cannes through the festival's closing ceremony, continuing meetings with international producers. The *Dada* biopic is expected to begin production later this year. As for his own next directorial project — whether in Hindi, English, or some language he hasn't learned yet — that remains deliciously uncertain. With Anurag Kashyap, it usually is.
